tldr: The authors propose a data foundation that integrates high-precision real-world 3D scanned environments (1,589 scenes) and egocentric human behavior data (4,230 recordings) in a shared absolute coordinate system, enabling the mass generation of simulation environments and high-quality full-body robot trajectories without deploying physical robots or motion-capture setups on site.
hero_caption: On the left are the acquired 3D scans and egocentric behavior data; on the right are the four robot learning applications derived from them. This structure illustrates how a single capture of a real environment scales diverse robot data at low cost, expanding into digital twin construction, human motion retargeting to robot trajectories, VR teleoperation, and automated long-horizon task generation.
overview:
While large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly by scaling data and model size, a major challenge in Physical AI—operating robots in physical space—has been how to establish similar scaling laws. Tackling complex, long-horizon real-world tasks requires both behavioral demonstrations showing "how to act" and interactive environments where policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. However, conventional methods of bringing physical robots on site for teleoperation or setting up motion-capture infrastructure are prohibitively expensive, labor-intensive, and fail to scale.

To address this, the authors developed "Ropedia Xperience 2," a framework in which an operator simply walks through everyday spaces equipped with a handheld LiDAR scanner and a head-mounted multi-camera recorder to simultaneously collect spatial geometry and human behaviors. Without using physical robots or external sensors, they collected 1,589 real-world scans and 4,230 egocentric activity logs across 74 distinct tasks (131 hours).

Furthermore, using a custom registration pipeline, they successfully aligned detailed human head, body, and hand motions, as well as video footage, onto the metric-scale 3D meshes and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes. They demonstrated that scanned rooms can be converted directly into physically interactive simulation environments (digital twins), complex human tasks can be accurately mapped to whole-body trajectories for wheeled humanoid robots, and long-horizon 8-step task trajectories can be generated autonomously in simulation. This approach of jointly capturing and repurposing real environments and human behaviors strongly suggests a new gold standard for scaling Physical AI.
contributions: Established a protocol to capture 3D real-world geometry and human behavior concurrently at scale using only a single operator with a handheld LiDAR scanner and a head-mounted camera, without physical robots or external motion-capture infrastructure on site.
Constructed an automated registration pipeline to accurately align 1,589 released 3D scene scans and 4,230 egocentric activity logs into a shared metric-scale coordinate system.

Demonstrated four robot data scaling routes, including Real-to-Sim conversion from real scans into interactive physical simulation environments and motion retargeting from human whole-body and hand motions to wheeled humanoid robot trajectories.

sections.heading: Scaling Physical AI Demands Both Environments and Behaviors
sections.summary: Although foundation models that directly control robots from vision have emerged, they remain brittle on real-world, long-horizon contact-rich tasks. Scaling capability requires behavioral demonstrations and interactive trial-and-error environments, and this paper presents a data foundation that captures and repurposes both without physical robots.
sections.details:
Recent foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have shown the potential to control robots directly from visual observations. For example, on the 42-task "RoboDojo" benchmark, GPT-6 Astra achieved an average success rate of 22.48%, outperforming dedicated robot policies. However, on real-world plug insertion tasks, it succeeded in 0 out of 11 trials, and in navigation & exploration, it succeeded in only 9 out of 23 trials, indicating that practical real-world deployment is still far off.

Why are they so brittle? The primary reason is an acute shortage of data allowing robots to interact with diverse environments and perform complex tasks in the real world. While language models followed clean scaling laws governing performance, data volume, and compute, establishing scaling laws for Physical AI requires answering which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously at low cost.

To address this, the paper proposes "Ropedia Xperience 2." It combines metric 3D scans capturing real-world environments via LiDAR with egocentric activity recordings collected using a head-mounted multi-camera system called "HOMIE." Crucially, neither physical robots nor external motion-capture cameras are brought to the capture site. An operator simply walks around, yielding spatial geometric structure alongside full-body and hand motions.

Furthermore, by integrating these into a shared absolute-scale coordinate frame, the collection becomes more than a static dataset—it turns into an asset for robot learning. Specifically, it enables four routes: (1) "Real-to-Sim" converting scanned spaces into physical simulation, (2) "Retargeting" mapping human movements to robot joint trajectories, (3) "Virtual Teleoperation" via VR in the simulator, and (4) "Long-Horizon Trajectory Generation" automatically synthesizing multi-step tasks.

captions.F2: How collected 3D scans (meshes, 3DGS) and HOMIE behavior data (camera trajectories, hand/body poses, language instructions, etc.) connect to four robot learning applications. It emphasizes that, compared to physical robot teleoperation (such as DROID), environmental diversity and behavioral horizons can be scaled drastically while keeping collection costs down.

sections.heading: Recording Everyday Spaces and Human Actions Completely Robot-Free
sections.summary: In real-world living spaces including homes, shops, and offices, spatial scanning with a handheld LiDAR scanner and task recording with the head-mounted HOMIE camera were performed in two phases. Natural human tasks were acquired with high precision across 74 domestic and operational activities.
sections.details:
The data collection aims to capture how humans naturally interact with their surroundings alongside the 3D geometry of the environment.

### Sensor Specialization
Completely capturing the shape of a whole space requires a sensor with flexible viewpoints, whereas recording a person at work demands hands-free operation and cameras that track their line of sight. Therefore, two dedicated hardware systems with distinct roles were adopted:
- **3D Scanner**: A handheld LiDAR device equipped with two fisheye cameras and two wide-angle cameras, allowing operators to walk around and scan occluded spots like high surfaces and narrow furniture gaps.
- **HOMIE (Head-Mounted Multi-Camera Recorder)**: A head-mounted device with two forward-facing and two backward-facing global-shutter fisheye cameras. The front stereo pair reliably captures hands and objects during tasks without rolling-shutter artifacts even under aggressive head motions. It also incorporates a 200 Hz IMU and a 4-channel microphone.

### 2.1 Scene and Task Design
Capture locations span private residences, restaurants, stores, offices, and outdoor scenes. First, a scene (Level 1) is selected, and multiple tasks (Level 2) are assigned to it. There are 74 task types in total, centered around everyday actions in homes and shops, such as "place / take out (25 types)," "wipe / clean (23 types)," and "organize / tidy (18 types)." The majority of the 4,230 task logs were collected in residential settings like bedrooms, living rooms, and bathrooms.

### 2.2 Rigorous Capture Protocol
To standardize data quality, collection followed a structured standard operating procedure. During the preparation phase, the room state was kept static from the start of the 3D scan until task recording finished. Lighting was held constant, screens were turned off, bystanders and pets were cleared, and transparent surfaces like glass windows were covered if necessary. Next, the operator walked slowly back and forth across routes, overlapping passes across high and low vantage points. Finally, the operator donned the HOMIE rig and performed the assigned tasks naturally, one by one. Multiple task recordings are linked to each single spatial scan.

captions.F3: The data collection pipeline: (a) pre-defining multiple tasks for the target space, (b) scanning the full room geometry once with the handheld LiDAR scanner without occlusions, and (c) naturally performing and recording each task in the same room wearing the HOMIE head-mounted camera.

sections.heading: Unifying Vision, Motion, and Language into a Metric Coordinate Frame
sections.summary: Meshes, 3D Gaussian Splatting models, camera trajectories, hand and body joint poses, and hierarchical language annotations are automatically extracted from the raw data. A registration technique was also established to precisely align the egocentric logs into the 3D scanned spaces.
sections.details:
Because raw sensor logs cannot be directly fed into learning algorithms, an automated pipeline converts them into rich multimodal assets.

### 3.1 3D Scan Processing
From the scanner data, the pipeline outputs COLMAP-format images with camera poses, triangular meshes, and photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. Because they are grounded in LiDAR measurements, everything is unified in an absolute metric scale (scene coordinate frame).

### 3.2 HOMIE Recording Processing
- **Synchronization and Calibration**: The four cameras are hardware-synchronized within 50 microseconds and managed under shared frame indices at 30 fps. The 200 Hz IMU data is also precisely aligned via timestamps.
- **Camera Trajectory and Depth**: Front stereo images are rectified, and gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories are estimated via SLAM. Simultaneously, stereo matching computes metric depth per pixel alongside confidence maps.
- **Hand and Body Pose Estimation**: Hand motion is modeled using MANO, estimating 21 joint positions per hand with high accuracy via stereo keypoint detection and reprojection consistency. Full-body motion builds on EgoAllo, fitting SMPL-H models (52 joints at 30 Hz) constrained by the SLAM head trajectory and estimated hand positions. Unobserved body parts, such as the legs, are plausibly inferred using a learned human motion prior.
- **Hierarchical Language Annotation**: Using large multimodal models, detailed language captions are generated across three temporal scales: high-level summaries of the overall task, sub-task and action segment descriptions, and frame-level object states and hand-object interactions.

### 3.3 Scan-to-Egocentric Registration
This step is technically critical. HOMIE's SLAM coordinate frame is independent of the scan's scene frame. To align them, SIFT features extracted from HOMIE frames are matched to 3D keypoints back-projected onto the scan mesh via Perspective-n-Point (PnP) for initial pose estimation. Next, camera centers from roughly 200 representative frames are robustly aligned using the Umeyama algorithm. In addition, alignments are strictly verified—checking agreement between IMU gravity and scan floor normals, verifying feet contact with the floor, and measuring ICP error between stereo depth and the mesh—and only reliable alignments receive a passing grade (PASS).

captions.F5: An egocentric recording registered into 3DGS space. In the top row, the human full-body skeleton (orange/blue), past and future head-camera trajectories, egocentric views, and language annotations are fully synchronized. The bottom row shows a 45-second trajectory in a different room, demonstrating that spatial relationships to furniture and floorplans are reconstructed consistently at millimeter-to-centimeter precision.

sections.heading: Thorough Quality Control and Open Release of 1,589 Scenes
sections.summary: Rigorous quality control (QC) was conducted on the collected scans, resulting in 1,589 publicly released scenes. Approximately 99% met usable standards, with an extensive lineup concentrated primarily across diverse domestic rooms.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Dataset Scale
This dataset significantly expands and advances upon the prior "Xperience-10M" collection of 10 million egocentric video clips. Across the full inventory, 4,230 task recordings (131 hours) were gathered across 596 unique locations. From these, 1,589 fully processed and QC-approved 3D scene scans were officially released.

### 4.2 Quality Control (QC) Grading Criteria
Visual and geometric inspections were conducted across 1,610 completed scans. As a result, 98.7% (1,589 scenes) were retained, while only 21 scenes (1.3%) with severe issues were discarded (Delete).
- **Perfect (148 scenes, 9.3%)**: Flawlessly passed all five QC check items, exhibiting pristine geometry and textures with zero reconstruction artifacts.
- **Usable (934 scenes, 58.8%)**: Fully cover the entire room, with minor local texture blur or slight noise, but entirely suitable for robot learning and benchmarking.
- **Reuse (507 scenes, 31.9%)**: Contain partial scan holes or local imperfections, but observed regions remain individually usable without issue.
- **Delete (21 scenes, 1.3%)**: Geometry corrupted due to moving doors during scanning (12 cases), reconstruction failures (8 cases), or dynamic interference from passing pedestrians/vehicles (1 case); all excluded from the release.

Looking at the distribution, residential interiors represent 1,389 scans (87.4%), with bedrooms and living rooms alone accounting for 61.4% of the total. In addition, 152 outdoor scans are included, where 86.2% of outdoor corridor scenes maintain a quality rating of Usable or better.

captions.F6: Quality control (QC) distribution and representative examples of each grade. 98.7% of the scans were accepted, and only scans with physical inconsistencies—such as doors moving mid-scan—were strictly rejected as 'Delete'.

sections.heading: From Scans to Physical AI: Benchmarking and Repurposing for Robot Learning
sections.summary: Using the high-precision 3D scans as ground truth, three spatial intelligence benchmarks were evaluated. Furthermore, four downstream robot learning applications were validated: Real-to-Sim conversion, humanoid motion retargeting, VR teleoperation, and autonomous long-horizon trajectory generation.
sections.details:
To demonstrate the value of this dataset, empirical evaluations were conducted in two directions: benchmarking existing AI models and repurposing assets for robot learning.

### 5.1 Benchmarking Existing Models
Across 20 shared evaluation scenes, models were tested on three tasks:
- **Depth and Geometry Estimation**: Evaluated across Sparse (5 images), Medium (11–100 images), and Dense (335–500 images) inputs, $\pi^3$ achieved the lowest trajectory error and highest surface reconstruction accuracy (5 cm F-score). However, models like DUSt3R and MASt3R crashed with out-of-memory (OOM) errors as image counts scaled up, highlighting scalability challenges on dense inputs.
- **3D Object Detection**: Tested against manually annotated 3D bounding boxes. Boxer, which lifts 2D open-vocabulary detections into 3D, achieved the top score; however, AP at IoU 0.5 (AP50) remained below 7% for all models, underscoring the extreme difficulty of accurate 3D detection in cluttered real-world rooms.
- **Spatial Reasoning (Spatial Intelligence)**: Evaluated across 500 spatial Q&A questions, Gemini-2.5-Pro achieved the highest accuracy (74.2%). While all models scored over 74% on height and relative position queries, accuracy on absolute metric distance estimation peaked at only 34%, revealing that metric distance reasoning remains a fundamental bottleneck for current VLMs.

### 5.2 Four Routes to Robot Learning
Scanned environments and behavior logs were repurposed into core assets for robot learning:
- **Real-to-Sim**: From a single scan, a digital twin containing 217 articulated and rigid interactive objects (furniture, appliances) was constructed in a physics simulator. Grounded in absolute LiDAR scale, the visual 3DGS models match the underlying physics collision meshes exactly, unlike reconstructions from uncalibrated images.
- **Human-Robot Retargeting**: Human task logs (10.3 minutes, 96 meters traversed) were retargeted to whole-body trajectories for a wheeled humanoid robot. The retargeting stayed within 90% of robot joint velocity/torque limits, kept the Zero Moment Point (ZMP) within the support polygon, and achieved median end-effector tracking errors of just 0.40–0.55 cm.
- **Virtual Teleoperation**: Operators wearing VR headsets entered a Real-to-Sim kitchen to teleoperate the humanoid robot to grasp a kettle, lift it, navigate to the stove, and place it. Beyond eliminating physical hardware, object layouts can be reset instantaneously in simulation, dramatically increasing data collection throughput.
- **Long-Horizon Trajectory Generation**: An 8-stage continuous sequential task was orchestrated in simulation: pick a mug in the kitchen, open the microwave, place it inside, close the door, run the cycle, open the door, retrieve the mug, close the door, push open the bedroom door, and place the mug on the nightstand. Tested across 30 varied initial configurations, all runs (30/30) successfully completed without dropping the mug or violating constraints. Generating a single trajectory took 10–16 minutes of computation, demonstrating that high-quality long-horizon demonstrations can scale unboundedly with compute.

captions.F9: Whole-body retargeting results from egocentric logs to a wheeled humanoid robot. For continuous human activities involving walking, doing laundry, clearing dishes, and operating an air conditioner, the robot's median fingertip tracking error remained tiny at 0.40–0.55 cm, passing all tip-over and joint limit checks.

sections.heading: Key Limitations and Future Directions
sections.summary: The paper candidly discusses constraints that users should bear in mind, such as the bias toward residential spaces, the presence of partial holes in some scans, and the fact that human motion estimates are algorithmic rather than optical motion-capture ground truth.
sections.details:
When utilizing this dataset, several limitations must be considered:

- **Environmental Bias and Incomplete Reconstructions**: 87.4% of released scans are residential interiors, with limited diversity in industrial or commercial domains. Additionally, the "Reuse" grade (roughly 30% of scans) exhibits partial holes or local distortions, meaning full room coverage is not guaranteed for every scene.
- **Nature of Motion Annotations**: Human hand and body poses are not ground truth measured via marker-based optical motion capture; they are inferred from SLAM trajectories and stereo images via algorithms (EgoAllo and MANO fitting). Out-of-view joints, such as the legs, rely heavily on learned motion priors.
- **Local SLAM Drift**: Because registration between scans and egocentric recordings relies on rigid or similarity transformations, local SLAM drift accumulating over long recording trajectories cannot be fully resolved by a single global alignment matrix.

sections.heading: Technical Deep Dive: Sensor Sync and Geometric Registration
sections.summary: This section details the microsecond-level hardware synchronization and camera calibration of the HOMIE device, as well as the rigorous PnP and Umeyama alignment pipeline used to register egocentric SLAM trajectories into 3D scanned spaces.
sections.details:
### B.1 Sensor Synchronization and Coordinate Frames
The four fisheye cameras on HOMIE are hardware-synchronized via trigger signals within 50 microseconds. Calibration keeps reprojection errors below 0.5 pixels across 1920×1088 sensor images. Front stereo images are rectified into pinhole images (cropped to 1452×824), serving as the geometric foundation for metric depth estimation and hand keypoint tracking.

### B.3 Scan-to-Behavior Registration Pipeline
The estimation of the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ mapping HOMIE's SLAM frame into the scan's scene coordinate frame is designed to be highly robust:
1. **Global Initialization**: SIFT features from texture-rich frames are matched against 3D scan points to estimate an initial camera pose via RANSAC fundamental matrix estimation and PnP.
2. **Local Tracking and Fitting**: PnP registration to the scan geometry is repeated across roughly 200 evenly spaced frames throughout the recording. The resulting camera centers are fitted using a robust Umeyama algorithm to solve for a similarity (with scale) or rigid transformation. Scale adjustment is permitted only if the trajectory exceeds 2.5 m and validation error is decisively reduced; otherwise, it is constrained to a rigid transform to prevent artificial deformation.
3. **Independent Verification and Acceptance**: Alignments undergo multiple validation checks, including the angle between IMU gravity and scan floor normals, foot contact elevation relative to the floor plane, and ICP (Iterative Closest Point) residuals between stereo depth maps and the scan mesh. If the ICP correction exceeds 30 cm, it indicates a visual match with mismatched underlying 3D geometry, and the registration is rejected (FAIL).

takeaways: High-quality multimodal environment and behavior data suitable for robot learning can be gathered at scale using only an operator with a handheld LiDAR scanner and a head-mounted camera, without physical robots or mocap infrastructure on site.

Constructing interactive physics-based simulation environments (digital twins) from real-world scans enables the computational amplification of behavioral data through VR teleoperation and fully autonomous multi-step trajectory generation.

Binding absolute metric geometry (LiDAR) and egocentric human behavior within a shared coordinate system establishes a standard platform for data collection and scaling law investigations in Physical AI.
limitations: The dataset is predominantly biased toward residential environments, with ongoing work required to expand into industrial facilities, commercial stores, and outdoor domains.

Human hand and body motions are algorithmic estimates from imagery rather than ground-truth sensor measurements, leaving ambiguities inherent to learned priors during occlusions like lower-body movements.
When egocentric SLAM accumulates local drift over long recordings, global rigid-body transformations cannot fully absorb localized geometric distortions.
